To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Asian central banks have to choose between two incompatible policy objectives: either to keep their pegs or to diversify their reserves.

the dollar would weaken if Asian central banks would diversify their reserves from dollar into yen or euro, and that the dollar would strengthen if Asian central banks shift from intervening against dollar to intervening against euro.

1) Asian currency pegs are incompatible with the diversification of Asian reserves from dollar into other currencies, and 2) Asian currency peg is incompatible with Asian interventions against the dollar, and compatible with interventions against the euro.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the consequences of Asian foreign exchange market operations on the exchange rates of the three most important currencies.
the question of how the euro can be strengthened against the dollar and yen in a way which is compatible with Asian currency pegging.
the question of whether Asian countries can maintain their dollar pegs while at the same time diversifying their reserves away from dollar assets into euro and yen assets.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

Asian central bank operations are not the cause of the dollar's weakness, but that they are a symptom of a more fundamental cause, namely that the euro has become a major international reserve currency.
Asian currency pegs are incompatible with the current euro-dollar-yen exchange rate regime.
the dollar would benefit from Asian interventions against the dollar and euro, and that the dollar would suffer from a diversification of Asian reserves into euro.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the dollar is the key currency of the Bretton Woods system and Asian central banks are not in a position to alter this situation.
Asian currency pegs are incompatible with a diversification of Asian reserves into euro.
Asian central banks should not intervene in the foreign exchange market.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a diversification from dollar into euro is not a solution for Asian central banks to reduce their dollar dependence.
Asian central banks are not only constrained by their currency pegs but by the portfolio composition as well.
the dollar is not the main currency in the Asian currency peg system but the euro.
